verses.zh: （大卫的诗。）耶和华―我的磐石是应当称颂的！他教导我的手争战，教导我的指头打仗。
verses.en: By David.The Lord, my Protector,[NOTE:1] deserves praise[NOTE:2]—the one who trains my hands for battle[NOTE:3] and my fingers for war,
notes: Psalm 144. The psalmist expresses his confidence in God, asks for a mighty display of divine intervention in an upcoming battle, and anticipates God’s rich blessings on the nation in the aftermath of military victory.
Heb “my rocky summit.” The Lord is compared to a rocky summit where one can find protection from enemies. See Ps 18:2.
Heb “blessed [be] the Lord, my rocky summit.”
verses.commentary:
144:1-4 This strophe uses numerous
military allusions. This is obviously a royal Psalm. YHWH acts on behalf of His
people to assure their survival because He has a universal redemptive plan
involving national Israel (the descendants of Abraham).

Psalm 144:3-4 is surprising in that the focus moves from Israel
to all humans.

- they are the object of YHWH's special care (cf. Ps. 8:4) because they are made in His image and likeness (cf. Gen. 1:26-27)

- however, because of Genesis 3 they are frail and finite (cf. Ps. 90:5; 103:15; 104:14; Isa. 40:6-8; 1 Pet. 1:24)

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

verses.zh: 他是我慈爱的主，我的山寨，我的高台，我的救主，我的盾牌，是我所投靠的；他使我的百姓服在我以下。
verses.en: who loves me[NOTE:1] and is my stronghold,my refuge[NOTE:2] and my deliverer,my shield and the one in whom I take shelter,who makes nations submit to me.[NOTE:3]
notes: The one who trains my hands for battle. The psalmist attributes his skill with weapons to divine enablement (see Ps 18:34). Egyptian reliefs picture gods teaching the king how to shoot a bow. See O. Keel, The Symbolism of the Biblical World, 265.
Heb “my loyal love,” which is probably an abbreviated form of “the God of my loyal love” (see Ps 59:10, 17).
Or “my elevated place.”
verses.commentary:
144:2 My lovingkindness" YHWH is
faithful in His covenant commitments.

Notice the number of PERSONAL PRONOUNS in the NASB
of Ps. 144:1-2 (six). The psalmist knows and trusts YHWH.

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS (hesed)

▣ "refuge" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: REFUGE

▣

NASB, NKJV, LXX
"Who subdues my people under me"

NRSV, TEV, Targums, Peshitta, Vulgate
"who subdues the peoples under me"

NJB
"He makes the peoples submit to me"

The difference is only a final mem. The UBS Text Project
(p. 436) gives "my people" a "B" rating (some doubt). This line of poetry either

- asserts the king's authority over the covenant people (i.e., he is YHWH's under shepherd)

- asserts Israel's victory by YHWH's power over the pagan nations

The UBS Text Project (p. 437) gives "under me" an "A" rating
(very high probability). If this is the correct text, then option #1 above is
the correct implication.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，人算甚么，你竟认识他！世人算甚么，你竟顾念他！
verses.en: O Lord, of what importance is the human race[NOTE:1] that you should notice them?Of what importance is mankind[NOTE:2] that you should be concerned about them?[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the one who subdues nations beneath me.”
Heb “What is mankind?” The singular noun אֱנוֹשׁ (ʾenosh) is used here in a collective sense and refers to the human race. See Ps 8:5.

Heb “and the son of man.” The phrase “son of man” is used here in a collective sense and refers to human beings. For other uses of the phrase in a collective or representative manner, see Num 23:19; Ps 146:3; Isa 51:12.
verses.commentary:
144:3 Notice the synonymous parallelism.

- "man" ‒ Adam (BDB 9)

- "son of man" ‒ "ben enosh" (BDB 60)

In the parallel in Psalm 8 the Hebrew words for "man" are
reversed, but the intent is the same. These terms are speaking of a human
person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SON OF MAN

▣ "take knowledge" This is the Hebrew VERB "know"
(BDB 393, KB 390, Qal PERFECT with waw).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

verses.zh: 人好像一口气；他的年日如同影儿快快过去。
verses.en: People[NOTE:1] are like a vapor,their days like a shadow that disappears.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “take account of him.” The two imperfect verbal forms in v. 4 describe God’s characteristic activity.
Heb “man,” or “mankind.”
verses.commentary:
144:4 This verse highlights the
finitude of mankind (cf. Job 8:9; 14:2; Ps. 39:5-6; 102:11; 109:23; Eccl. 6:12;
8:12) and although not specifically stated, the eternality of YHWH is
highlighted.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你使天下垂，亲自降临，摸山，山就冒烟。
verses.en: O Lord, make the sky sink[NOTE:1] and come down.[NOTE:2] Touch the mountains and make them smolder.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “his days [are] like a shadow that passes away,” that is, like a late afternoon shadow made by the descending sun that will soon be swallowed up by complete darkness. See Ps 102:11.

The Hebrew verb נָטָה (natah) can carry the sense “to [cause to] bend; to [cause to] bow down.” For example, Gen 49:15 pictures Issachar as a donkey that “bends” its shoulder or back under a burden. Here the Lord causes the sky, pictured as a dome or vault, to sink down as he descends in the storm. See Ps 18:9.
Heb “so you might come down.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose after the preceding imperative. The same type of construction is utilized in v. 6.
verses.commentary:
144:5-8 This strophe is a series of
prayer requests. It is surprising in light of Ps. 144:1-4. The psalmist asserts
YHWH's power and presence in the first strophe but pleads for His deliverance in
this one.

Note the IMPERATIVES and IMPERFECTS
used in an IMPERATIVAL sense.

- bow, Ps. 144:5 (lit. "bend") ‒ BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil IMPERATIVE, cf. Ps. 8:9

- come down, Ps. 144:5 ‒ BDB 432, KB 434, Qal IMPERFECT but used as
IMPERATIVAL prayer request

- touch, Ps. 144:5 ‒ BDB 619, KB 668, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Ps. 104:32

- flash forth, Ps. 144:6 ‒ BDB 140, KB 162, Qal IMPERATIVE

- scatter (i.e., arrows on alien invaders), Ps. 144:6 ‒ BDB 806, KB 918, Hiphil
IMPERFECT used as IMPERATIVAL prayer request

- send out, Ps. 144:6 ‒ BDB 1018, KB 1511, Qal IMPERATIVE

- confuse, Ps. 144:6 ‒ BDB 243, KB 251, Qal IMPERFECT used as
IMPERATIVAL prayer request

- stretch forth, Ps. 144:7 ‒ same as #6

- rescue (lit. "open," cf. Ps. 144:11), Ps. 144:7 ‒ BDB 822, KB 953, Qal
IMPERATIVE

- deliver me, Ps. 144:7 ‒ BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

144:5-7 These verses use "Holy War"
imagery to request YHWH' presence and power in battle. He will either

- train and empower the Israeli soldiers (Ps. 144:1)

- fight on Israel's behalf as in the conquest of Canaan under Joshua (Ps. 144:6)

verses.zh: 求你发出闪电，使他们四散，射出你的箭，使他们扰乱。
verses.en: Hurl lightning bolts and scatter the enemy.Shoot your arrows and rout them.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “so they might smolder.” The prefixed verbal form with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates purpose after the preceding imperative.
verses.commentary:
144:6 "Lighting. . .arrows" These images of YHWH's military power are in a parallel relationship
(cf. Ps. 18:14; 77:17-18; Zech. 9:14).

▣

NASB
"confuse them"

NKJV, Peshitta
"destroy them"

NRSV, NJB, JPSOA
"rout them"

TEV
"send them running"

LXX
"throw them into disarray"

There are two possible Hebrew roots.

- המם, BDB 243, KB 251, "rout," cf. 2 Sam. 22:15; Ps. 18:14

- הום, KB 242, confuse," this one has "Holy War" connotation,
cf. Josh. 10:10; Jdgs. 4:15; 1 Sam. 7:10; 2 Chr. 15:6

verses.zh: 求你从上伸手救拔我，救我出离大水，救我脱离外邦人的手。
verses.en: Reach down[NOTE:1] from above.Grab me and rescue me from the surging water,[NOTE:2] from the power of foreigners[NOTE:3]
notes: Arrows and lightning bolts are associated in other texts (see Pss 18:14; 77:17-18; Zech 9:14), as well as in ancient Near Eastern art (see R. B. Chisholm, “An Exegetical and Theological study of Psalm 18/2 Samuel 22” [Th.D. diss., Dallas Theological Seminary, 1983], 187).
Heb “stretch out your hands.”
Heb “mighty waters.” The waters of the sea symbolize the psalmist’s powerful foreign enemies, as well as the realm of death they represent (see the next line and Ps 18:16-17).
verses.commentary:
144:7 Notice "great waters" is
parallel to "the hand of aliens." The imagery is from

- chaos of creation, cf. Job 41:1-11; Ps. 74:12-17; Isa. 51:9-10; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: WATERS

- invasion, cf. Ps. 18:16-17; Isa. 17:12-14; 28:2; Jer. 51:34

- death, cf. Ps. 18:4-6

verses.zh: 他们的口说谎话；他们的右手起假誓。
verses.en: who speak liesand make false promises.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “from the hand of the sons of foreignness.”
verses.commentary:
144:8 The "aliens" (BDB 648, KB 700 I) are
characterized as those who lie. One's words reveal one's heart. This seems to
refer to international treaties or possibly court testimony under oath (cf. Gen.
14:22; Deut. 32:40; Ps. 106:26; Isa. 44:20). YHWH is true to His word (cf. Ps.
144:2a), but pagans and some Israelites are not!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH

verses.zh: 神啊，我要向你唱新歌，用十弦瑟向你歌颂。
verses.en: O God, I will sing a new song to you.Accompanied by a ten-stringed instrument, I will sing praises to you,
verses.commentary:
144:9-11 This strophe has three emphases.

- what the psalmist promises to do

- I will sing a new song to God, Ps. 144:9a ‒ BDB 1010, KB 1479, Qal
COHORTATIVE (i.e., composed to celebrate YHWH's victory)

- I will sing praises to God, Ps. 144:9b ‒ BDB 274, KB 273, Piel
COHORTATIVE

- YHWH's past acts of deliverance

- He delivered Israel's Kings, Ps. 144:10a

- He delivered David, Ps. 144:10b (probably kings of David's line)

- the psalmist's prayer is based on YHWH's previous acts

- rescue me, Ps. 144:11a ‒ BDB 822, KB 963, Qal IMPERATIVE

- deliver me, Ps. 144:11a ‒ BDB 664, KB 717, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

Notice the parallel between Ps. 144:7-8 and 144:11.

144:9 "God" This is the title Elohim.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

verses.zh: 你是那拯救君王的；你是那救仆人大卫脱离害命之刀的。
verses.en: the one who delivers[NOTE:1] kingsand rescued David his servant from a deadly[NOTE:2] sword.
notes: Heb “who [with] their mouth speak falsehood, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” The reference to the “right hand” is probably a metonymy for an oath. When making an oath, one would raise the hand as a solemn gesture. See Exod 6:8; Num 14:30; Deut 32:40. The figure thus represents the making of false oaths (false promises).
Heb “grants deliverance to.”
verses.commentary:
144:10 "salvation" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SALVATION (OT)

▣ "David His servant" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: MY SERVANT

▣ "from the evil sword" This is
an unusual characterization. Several translations put the phrase in the next
line of poetry (i.e., NRSV, TEV, NJB). Other translations have

- REB ‒ "the cruel sword"

- JPSOA ‒ "the deadly sword"

- KJV, Peshitta ‒ "the hurtful sword"

- AB ‒ "the sword of the Evil One"

- NAB ‒ "the menacing sword"

In context it seems to relate to the "aliens" (Ps. 144:7c,
11a). The Aramaic Targums (translation with comments) interpreted it as "from
the evil sword of Goliath" (UBS Handbook, p. 1159).

verses.zh: 求你救拔我，救我脱离外邦人的手。他们的口说谎话；他们的右手起假誓。
verses.en: Grab me and rescue me from the power of foreigners[NOTE:1] who speak liesand make false promises.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “harmful.”
Heb “from the hand of the sons of foreignness.”

verses.zh: 我们的儿子从幼年好像树栽子长大；我们的女儿如同殿角石，是按建宫的样式凿成的。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] our sons will be like plants,that quickly grow to full size.[NOTE:2] Our daughters will be like corner pillars,[NOTE:3] carved like those in a palace.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “who [with] their mouth speak falsehood, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.” See v. 8 where the same expression occurs.

Some consider אֲשֶׁר (ʾasher) problematic, but here it probably indicates the anticipated consequence of the preceding request. (For other examples of אֲשֶׁר indicating purpose/result, see BDB 83 s.v. and HALOT 99 s.v.) If the psalmist—who appears to be a Davidic king preparing to fight a battle (see vv. 10-11)—is victorious, the whole nation will be spared invasion and defeat (see v. 14) and can flourish. Some prefer to emend the form to אַשְׁרֵי (“how blessed [are our sons]”). A suffixed noun sometimes follows אַשְׁרֵי (ʾashre; see 1 Kgs 10:8; Prov 20:7), but the presence of a comparative element (see “like plants”) after the suffixed noun makes the proposed reading too awkward syntactically.

Heb “grown up in their youth.” The translation assumes that “grown up” modifies “plants” (just as “carved” modifies “corner pillars” in the second half of the verse). Another option is to take “grown up” as a predicate in relation to “our sons,” in which case one might translate, “they will be strapping youths.”
The Hebrew noun occurs only here and in Zech 9:15, where it refers to the corners of an altar.
verses.commentary:
144:12-14 This strophe is
characterized by seven PARTICIPLES (1) used as JUSSIVES
(2) statements of fact.

- young sons as grown up plants, Ps. 144:12a ‒ BDB 152, KB 178, Pual

- young daughters as fashioned (lit. "hewn") pillars, Ps. 144:12b ‒ BDB 310, KB 306, Pual

- garners producing, Ps. 144:13a ‒ BDB 807, KB 920, Hiphil

- flocks bringing forth thousands, Ps. 144:13b ‒ BDB 48 II, KB 59, Hiphil (found only here)

- flocks bringing forth ten thousands, Ps. 144:13b ‒ BDB 912, KB 1174, Pual

- cattle bear (lit. be heavy with young), Ps. 144:14a ‒ BDB 687, KB 741, Pual

- going out (i.e., "bearing" ) with no problems, Ps. 144:14b ‒ BDB 422, KB 425, Qal

- there is an implied PARTICIPLE in Ps. 144:14c ‒ NASB has "let," which
matches Ps. 144:12-14b, "let there be no outcry in our streets"

These are all blessings of covenant obedience (cf. Leviticus
26; Deuteronomy 27-30). Notice the covenant blessing of Ps. 144:15. NASB
translates both Ps. 144:1 and 15 as "blessed," but they are different Hebrew
words.

- Ps. 144:1 ‒ BDB 138

- Ps. 144:15 ‒ BDB 80

The term "happy" or "blessed" (BDB 80, cf. Ps. 1:1) is recurrent and
describes why they are blessed (cf. Ps. 32:1-2; 34:8; 40:4; 84:5,12; 94:12;
127:5; Prov. 3:13; 8:34; 28:14). It is also used of corporate blessings (cf. Ps.
33:12; 89:15; 144:15).

144:12 The term "plants" (BDB 642)
occurs only here but it is very close to the normal root for "plant."

- plant (here) ‒ נטיע

- plant ‒ נטע, used often

▣ "corner pillars" This is also a rare
term, found only here and in Zech. 9:15.

verses.zh: 我们的仓盈满，能出各样的粮食；我们的羊在田间孳生千万。
verses.en: Our storehouses[NOTE:1] will be full,providing all kinds of food.[NOTE:2] Our sheep will multiply by the thousandsand fill[NOTE:3] our pastures.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “carved [in] the pattern of a palace.”
The Hebrew noun occurs only here.
Heb “from kind to kind.” Some prefer to emend the text to מָזוֹן עַל מָזוֹן (mazon ʿal mazon, “food upon food”).
Heb “they are innumerable.”
verses.commentary:
144:13 "garners" This term (BDB 265, KB
565) is also found only here in the OT (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 909). Most
translations have "barns."

verses.zh: 我们的牛驮着满驮，没有人闯进来抢夺，也没有人出去争战；我们的街市上也没有哭号的声音。
verses.en: Our cattle will be weighted down with produce.[NOTE:1] No one will break through our walls,no one will be taken captive,and there will be no terrified cries in our city squares.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “in outside places.” Here the term refers to pastures and fields (see Job 5:10; Prov 8:26).

Heb “weighted down.” This probably refers (1) to the cattle having the produce from the harvest placed on their backs to be transported to the storehouses (see BDB 687 s.v. סָבַל). Other options are (2) to take this as reference to the cattle being pregnant (see HALOT 741 s.v. סבל pu) or (3) to their being well-fed or fattened (see L. C. Allen, Psalms 101-150 [WBC], 288).
verses.commentary:
144:14 There are two ways to view this verse.

- It goes with Ps. 144:13b and relates to healthy, fruitful livestock (BDB 687, KB 741, Pual PARTICIPLE;
NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 498).

- It related to cattle carrying heavy loads of harvested crops (NET Bible, p. 1009, #8).

- It goes with Ps. 144:14b,c and relates to a prayer for no breach in the city wall, which would allow an invader entrance.

The UBS Handbook (p. 1161) asserts there is no way from the text or
context to know which option is best.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide
commentary which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of
the Bible. Each of us must walk n the light we have. You, the Bible, and the
Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a
commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think
through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be
thought provoking, not definitive.

- How is this Psalm related to Psalm 18?

- How do Ps. 144:3 and 4 relate to Ps. 144:1 and 2?

- How does Ps. 144:5-7 relate to "Holy War"?

- To what or whom does "great waters" in Ps. 144:7 refer?

- Why does the MT introduction not fit Ps. 144:10?

- Are Ps. 144:12-14 prayers or statements?
